common_name: BARI Kanthal-3 Jackfruit (Bangladeshi Year-Round Fruiting Jackfruit)

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring after all frost danger has passed, in deep, well-drained soil; BARI Kanthal-3 was selected from Chattogram Hill Tracts germplasm near Ramgarh and released by the Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute in 2014.

directions: This Bangladeshi selection breaks from the normal jackfruit pattern of a single short summer crop and instead sets fruit across roughly ten months of the year, with only a brief rest in the hottest part of summer. Plant a grafted tree in deep, well-drained soil in full sun and expect notably heavier cropping than a seasonal seedling tree once established, along with deep orange, carotenoid-rich flesh. Because fruit can form on the trunk and lower limbs almost continuously, keep the area beneath the canopy clear for easy harvest access year-round. Protect young trees from any cold exposure, since this cultivar carries the same frost sensitivity as the species.
sources: Bangladesh Agricultural Research Institute (BARI) variety release records

planting.note: Plant a grafted tree in spring in full sun on deep, well-drained soil; Ashwina is a GI-recognized (2023) late-season mango of the Chapainawabganj mango belt in Bangladesh.

directions: Ashwina is valued in Bangladesh for ripening weeks after most other mango cultivars have finished bearing, holding its large, dark green-to-black fruit on the tree into August. Grow a grafted tree in full sun on deep, well-drained soil and expect fruit in the 400-500 gram range with an unusual pineapple-forward flavor rather than typical sweet-mango notes. Because the fruit's late hold-on-tree habit is part of its value, avoid heavy pre-harvest irrigation changes that could trigger early drop. Protect the tree from frost and cold wind, as it has no cold tolerance beyond typical tropical mango limits.

common_name: BJRI Tossa Pat-7 Jute (MG-1 High-Yield Bangladeshi Fiber Jute)

planting.note: Direct sow once soil is reliably warm; BJRI Tossa Pat-7 (also known as MG-1) was released by the Bangladesh Jute Research Institute in 2017 via pure-line selection and is normally sown from early March to mid-April in Bangladesh.

directions: This Bangladeshi tossa jute release was bred specifically for bast fiber production and outperforms older varieties on fiber yield, strength, and luster rather than leaf eating quality. Broadcast or drill seed thickly into warm, fertile soil and keep it consistently moist, since dense stands and steady water are what push stems to grow tall and straight before fiber extraction. Plants reach harvest readiness about 100-120 days after sowing, at which point stalks are cut and retted in water to separate the bast fiber from the stem core. Thin overcrowded seedlings only lightly, since a tight stand actually improves stem straightness and fiber quality in this cultivar.

planting.note: Root stem cuttings in partial shade in moist, humus-rich soil with support for climbing; Mitha Paan is the sweet betel leaf landrace long associated with Moheshkhali Island in Cox's Bazar district, Bangladesh.

directions: Mitha Paan is the sweet-tasting betel leaf grown around Moheshkhali Island in southeastern Bangladesh, prized by growers for milder flavor than sharper 'jhal' types and for notably better resistance to leaf rot and leaf burn than many other regional betel strains. Root stem cuttings in partial shade and train the vine up a trellis or support pole in moist, humus-rich soil, mirroring the humid coastal growing conditions of its home region. Because disease resistance is one of its defining traits, this type tolerates the humid, close-planted baroj-style growing beds common in Bangladeshi betel cultivation better than more rot-prone varieties. Harvest individual leaves once the vine is established and keep the soil evenly moist without letting it become waterlogged.

common_name: Bombai Litchi (Bangladesh's Most Widely Grown Lychee)

planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring after frost risk passes; Bombai is the dominant commercial litchi cultivar of Dinajpur, Bangladesh, accounting for the large majority of orchard trees there.

directions: Bombai is the early-season litchi that dominates Bangladesh's main lychee-growing district of Dinajpur, typically ripening by the second week of May before most other cultivars begin. Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and give it the same cool-dry winter rest other lychees need to set flower buds. Fruit clusters are heart-shaped and carmine red at ripeness, each averaging only 18-20 grams, often with a small undeveloped secondary fruit attached near the stalk — a useful identifying trait distinct from the larger, later Bedana type. Harvest promptly once fully colored, since the short five- to six-week market window for Dinajpur litchi closes quickly each year.

planting.note: Plant a grafted or air-layered tree in spring after frost risk passes; Bedana is the premium late-season litchi of Dinajpur, Bangladesh, which received Geographical Indication recognition for the district.

directions: Bedana is regarded as Bangladesh's finest litchi, prized for fruit that is larger than most other local types and for seeds so shriveled and thin that the pulp-to-seed ratio runs extremely high, giving an unusually fleshy bite. It is a late variety, ripening in the last week of June after earlier Dinajpur cultivars like Bombai have already finished, so plan harvest timing accordingly. Grow on a grafted or air-layered tree of moderate stature in deep, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, and provide the same brief cool-dry rest period lychees need in late autumn to set flower buds reliably. Pick only once fruit is fully colored and the skin feels firm, since this cultivar's thin skin and high sugar content make overripe fruit prone to splitting.
